credentials: PhD, Physical Anthropology (University of Minnesota, 1971); Professor, Washington State University, 1968-1998
stance: Krantz didn't just believe Sasquatch was real -- he believed it was a specific animal with a specific family tree: a surviving population of Gigantopithecus blacki, a genuine giant Asian ape that mainstream science says went extinct in the Pleistocene, which he theorized evolved bipedalism and walked across the Bering Land Bridge into North America long before humans did. This wasn't armchair theorizing -- Krantz used to drive the back roads of the Pacific Northwest late at night with a rifle in the car, hoping to be the one person on Earth who could bring back an actual body and settle the question for good. When the 1969 'Cripplefoot' tracks turned up at Bossburg, Washington, showing a deformed right foot, Krantz became convinced almost overnight: he argued the dermal ridges and the way the toes spread differently under weight were exactly the kind of subtle, internally-consistent anatomical detail that no 1960s hoaxer could have faked, deformity and all. He ran the same forensic eye over the Patterson-Gimlin film, arguing that the walking creature's persistent knee-bend, its unusually high foot clearance, and its forward lean weren't stylistic choices for a costume -- they were what a real 500-plus-pound animal would biomechanically have to do to walk upright without destroying its own joints. He had zero patience for anything paranormal -- no UFOs, no telepathy, no interdimensional travel -- Sasquatch, to Krantz, was flesh, bone, and biology or it was nothing. And he was honest about the discipline's biggest weak spot: no bones. His answer was that finding the remains of any large, low-density wild animal -- a bear, a cougar, a wolf -- is already vanishingly rare in the wild, so the total absence of a Sasquatch skeleton wasn't the damning evidence people assumed. He believed only a real specimen, a body, would ever satisfy science -- and when he couldn't bring one back in life, he arranged to become one in death: his own skeleton was donated to the Smithsonian, and today stands on permanent display next to the skeleton of his beloved Irish Wolfhound, Clyde -- a final, oddly touching field specimen from a man who spent his whole career chasing one.
key_publications: Big Footprints: A Scientific Inquiry into the Reality of Sasquatch (1992); Bigfoot Sasquatch Evidence (1999); 'Anatomy and Dermatoglyphics of Three Sasquatch Footprints,' Cryptozoology 2 (1983): 53-81; 'A Reconstruction of the Skull of Gigantopithecus blacki...,' Cryptozoology 5 (1987): 24-39
archive_location: National Anthropological Archives, Smithsonian Institution (Collection NAA.2003-21) — 7.38 linear feet, 9 series including a dedicated 'Sasquatch, 1963-2001' series

credentials: PhD, Wildlife Biology (University of Wisconsin-Madison); BSc Biology (University of Guelph); wildlife biologist for UN FAO across Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean; curator, BFRO, until his death in 2018
stance: Bindernagel's whole approach came from a simple, stubborn idea: treat Sasquatch exactly like any other large, elusive mammal you'd study in the field, because that's what he'd spent his career doing -- tracking, watching, and habituating great apes and other large mammals in Africa and Asia for the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization. He wasn't a hobbyist who backed into science; he was a working wildlife biologist who moved his entire family to British Columbia in 1975 specifically because it was a sighting hotspot, the same way you'd relocate to study any animal in its actual range. What convinced him wasn't any single piece of evidence, but the pattern across hundreds of independent, unconnected witnesses: the same mid-tarsal foot-break biomechanics, the same chest-beating, the same wood-knocking, the same forward-slouched posture and specific vocalizations, described by people who had never met each other and had no reason to coordinate a story -- details, he argued, that an untrained eyewitness was extremely unlikely to invent from scratch because they were too specifically, correctly primate-like. He read footprint evidence the way a tracker reads sign: real dermal ridges and real weight-distribution patterns in the deep backcountry, he said, are exactly the kind of thing that make casual hoaxing implausible once you're far enough from a road. And he had a ready ecological answer for skeptics -- North America's vast, contiguous temperate forests carry more than enough biomass and cover to support a low-density, wide-ranging population without frequent human contact, the same as they do for actual documented large predators. On the missing-bones question, his answer mirrored Krantz's: finding the remains of any large, low-density wilderness animal is already genuinely rare, thanks to fast scavengers and acidic forest soil. But his sharpest argument came late, in his second book -- he turned the whole question around and argued the real obstacle was never a lack of evidence at all, but a scientific taboo: academics dismissing the subject as a hoax without ever formally appraising the evidence, which then lets them point to the lack of formal appraisal as proof it was never worth taking seriously in the first place -- a closed loop he spent his last book trying to break open.
key_publications: North America's Great Ape: The Sasquatch (1998); The Discovery of the Sasquatch: Reconciling Culture, History and Science in the Discovery Process (2010)
archive_location: No dedicated public archive identified. A full biography, 'Sasquatch Discovered: The Biography of Dr. John Bindernagel' by Terrance N. James (2022, Hancock House), likely draws on his personal papers as source material
archive_access: Not yet located as a standalone archive — the biography is the closest current access point to his working materials

credentials: Field investigator (no academic credential); major advocate for the Patterson-Gimlin film; acquired ownership rights over the film to protect and promote its research validity
stance: Dahinden was blunt, cranky, and impatient with anyone he thought was wasting the field's credibility -- and he spent nearly fifty years in the woods and courtrooms of the Pacific Northwest trying to protect it. He never once saw a Sasquatch himself, in half a century of looking, which makes what he actually did with his life more remarkable, not less: decades of fieldwork, tracking casts, and witness interviews across Western Canada and the US, done the hard way, on foot. For Dahinden, everything came down to one piece of film. He treated the 1967 Patterson-Gimlin footage as the single most important object in the entire field, and rather than just believing in it, he went and secured the actual copyright to it, then spent years bringing it to biomechanics experts and, tellingly, Hollywood costume designers -- professionals whose entire job was building convincing creature suits -- to make the case that nobody in 1967 could have built a suit that moved like that. He had no patience whatsoever for the paranormal wing of Bigfoot research -- to him this was a biological animal, evaluated with hard physical evidence and ordinary zoology, full stop -- and even less patience for hoaxers and fabricated plaster casts, which he called out loudly and often within the research community itself, making him as many enemies among believers as among skeptics. He was also clear-eyed about what it would actually take to win the argument: not eyewitness stories, however many of them piled up, but a type specimen -- a body, a bone, real tissue -- because he knew testimony alone would never move mainstream science. Near the end of his life, after four decades of searching without an answer, he said something to a friend that captures him better than anything else: 'You know, I've spent over 40 years -- and I didn't find it. I guess that's got to say something.' It's in his National Post obituary, and it reads less like defeat than like a man taking his own life's work seriously enough to be honest about where it actually landed.
key_publications: Sasquatch/Bigfoot (1993, co-authored with Don Hunter; originally published as Sasquatch, 1973)
archive_location: No dedicated public archive identified. Real correspondence with Krantz already surfaces in the Krantz Smithsonian collection (folder 0334, box 3). Loren Coleman's International Cryptozoology Museum (Portland, ME) holds materials connected to Dahinden as a personal correspondent

credentials: Journalist (University of British Columbia; MA Journalism, Columbia University); Royal Canadian Navy veteran; owner/editor, Agassiz-Harrison Advance; Mayor of Harrison Hot Springs; compiled a database of 3,000+ sighting/track reports
stance: Green's path into Sasquatch research started, fittingly for a small-town newspaperman, as a joke -- an April Fool's Day story he ran in the Agassiz-Harrison Advance about a Sasquatch kidnapping a woman from the local hotel. It's the kind of thing you'd forget about, except that within a few years the 'joke' became his life's work, and he approached it the only way he knew how: like a reporter, not a believer. He wanted signed affidavits, corroborating timelines, and actual print measurements before he'd take a report seriously -- the same standard he'd apply to any story running under his own newspaper's name -- and over the decades that discipline let him build something nobody else in the field had: a working database of more than 3,000 sighting and footprint reports, assembled entirely before the internet existed to make that easy. He put the most weight on trackways specifically, arguing that a set of deep, anatomically consistent, 15-inch-plus footprints stretched out over a long distance represented a real weight and a real stride pattern that would be nearly impossible for a hoaxer to fake continuously, step after step, without the pattern breaking down somewhere. He traveled to Bluff Creek himself and saw footprints as long as his own forearm -- an experience he still called formative decades later, at a 2011 tribute event held in his honor. He never hid his frustration that mainstream academia wouldn't seriously engage with the volume of evidence he'd personally catalogued, but he also kept a careful distance from the sensationalist, disorganized side of the field -- no gimmick expeditions, no showmanship. And he was candid about the strange position he was in: in fifty-plus years of chasing the story, he never once saw a Sasquatch himself. He called that a double-edged thing -- a real, lasting disappointment, but also, he believed, exactly what let him stay the field's most trusted, impartial chronicler instead of just another eyewitness with a story to defend.
